lesson.title: Verb Families & Root Radiations
lesson.subtitle: One root, many words: fahren/Fahrt, ziehen/Zug — like stand/understand/withstand

hook.title: The Root Is the Vocabulary
hook.content: English never gave you a list of 'stand-words': you own stand, understand, withstand, standstill, standout, 'I can't stand it' — one root, radiating. German does the same, visibly. fahren (to drive) radiates into die Fahrt (the journey), der Fahrer (the driver), das Fahrzeug (drive-stuff, a vehicle), abfahren (depart), ausfahren (drive out). ziehen (to pull) radiates into der Zug (the pull → the train!), der Aufzug (up-pull → elevator), der Umzug (move — the around-pull!), umziehen (to move house). Learn the root and the vocabulary grows itself.

footnotes.title: Zug, the Word That Pulls Everything
footnotes.content: der Zug means pull, draught, train, feature, and move — all from ziehen. A train is 'the puller'; a chess move is ein Zug; der Zeitgeist is the 'time-spirit'. One three-letter root pulls a whole semantic freight train — the way English 'draw' gives you drawer, withdraw, drawback, drawn-out.

pattern.title: Two Dynasties and a Method
pattern.content: The fahren dynasty: fahren, fuhr, gefahren ↔ fare, fared. Die Fahrt (the ride), der Fahrer (driver — the -er agent law!), das Fahrzeug (vehicle — the -zeug law), abfahren (depart — separable, prefix flies!), die Abfahrt (departure). The ziehen dynasty: ziehen, zog, gezogen ↔ tug, tugged? no — its English cousins are tow and tug. Der Zug (the train), der Aufzug (elevator), der Umzug (the move), umziehen (to move house), aufziehen (to raise). The method: when you meet a new German word, strip it to the root, check your Atlas family, then let the prefix and suffix laws name it for you.
pattern.linguist_note: ziehen's z is the T→Z shift of the ancient *teuhaną — the same root as English tow and tug. So der Zug, tow, and tug are one word: the train is named for pulling, exactly as a tugboat is.

exercises.prompt: Verb families — match each word with its meaning:
exercises.target_answer: die Fahrt, das Fahrzeug, abfahren, der Fahrer, gewinnen
exercises.meaning: the journey, the vehicle, to depart, the driver, to win
exercises.explanation: One root, four derivatives — every suffix law you own (-t, -zeug, separable, -er agent) is on display. gewinnen is ge- + winnen: the win-verb wearing its ancient prefix.

exercises.prompt: 'Der Zug fährt um acht.' — what is der Zug, literally?
options: The pull — the train is named for pulling
exercises.target_answer: The pull — the train is named for pulling
exercises.meaning: der Zug = the pull(er) = the train
exercises.explanation: ziehen → der Zug: the thing that pulls. An elevator is the up-pull (Aufzug), moving house the around-pull (Umzug). The city map radiates too: der Platz (the square), der Fluss (the river, flow's cousin), der Markt, die Wand (the wall — English's own wand, magic included) — nouns named by what they are.

exercises.prompt: The ziehen dynasty: 'Ich ___ nach Berlin um.' (I am moving — to Berlin; separable, verb-first):
exercises.english_hint: ziehen's root + the prefix at the end
exercises.meaning: Ich ziehe nach Berlin um = I am moving to Berlin
exercises.explanation: umziehen splits: ziehe in position 2, um at the end — and ziehen's z is the shifted t of tow/tug.

exercises.prompt: English runs the same radiation — which set matches the stehen family (verstehen, aufstehen)?
exercises.meaning: stehen ↔ stand: the radiation is identical
exercises.explanation: verstehen = understand (for-stand!), aufstehen = stand up. English and German built the same family from the same root. schauen (to look) runs its own show — die Schau, English show and scout — root radiations on both shores.

exercises.idea: you're planning a day trip: the journey takes an hour
cues: fahren's noun leads the sentence: die Fahrt — then dauert (the er/sie -t), and eine Stunde closes it

vocab_hints.note: dauern — related to 'endure'; the -t stays in the er-form
die Stunde — a distant cousin of 'stand' (the standing-time!)

exercises.explanation: die Fahrt — fahren's noun — as the subject, with a time expression in the accusative.

summary.outcome: Radiate fahren and ziehen into their noun families and read new words via roots.
summary.takeaway: Roots radiate: fahren → Fahrt/Fahrzeug/Fahrer; ziehen → Zug/Aufzug/Umzug — learn roots, not lists.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the fahren dynasty — one root radiating into Fahrt, Zug, and a whole transit system.

twist.prompt: Longer trip: the journey takes an hour becomes the journey takes A DAY. (Tag is masculine — mind the case.)
twist.explanation: eine Stunde → einen Tag: the time expression is accusative, and Tag is masculine — the Him-Case stamps the article. dauert and die Fahrt don't move.

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

fahrt.etymology_derivation: Noun of fahren (fare): a 'faring' — a drive, ride, or voyage; the -t is the Germanic -þ nominal suffix. [wiktionary]

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

ziehen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
ziehen.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (Proto-Germanic *teuhaną, cognate with English tow / tug).

nehmen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nemaną — the twin of archaic English nim 'to take', surviving in nimble ('quick to grasp'); English take is a Norse import. [wiktionary]

verstehen.etymology_derivation: Inseparable: ver- (for-) + stehen (stand). Past participle: verstanden (no ge-).

gewinnen.context_phrase: Unser Team will das Spiel gewinnen.
gewinnen.context_translation: Our team wants to win the game.
gewinnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *winnaną (PIE *wenh₁-) — English win descends from the same root (Old English winnan); strong verb: gewann, gewonnen. [wiktionary]

schauen.context_phrase: Wir schauen das Spiel im Fernsehen.
schauen.context_translation: We watch the game on TV.
schauen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (to look); the page cites Old English scēawian and compares English show — the old look-verb that English turned into show. [wiktionary]

platz.context_phrase: Der Platz vor dem Rathaus ist alt.
platz.context_translation: The square in front of the town hall is old.
platz.etymology_derivation: From Old French place, from Latin platea, from Greek plateia, broad way; the page names English place as a cognate — the same Latin-Greek square-word. [wiktionary]

fluss.context_phrase: Der Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
fluss.context_translation: The river flows through the city.
fluss.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German vluȥ, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, from the same root as fließen, to flow. English flow is the cognate of that root. [wiktionary]

markt.context_phrase: Auf dem Markt kaufe ich Obst.
markt.context_translation: At the market I buy fruit.
markt.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *markat, an early Latin borrowing shared with English market. [wiktionary]

wand.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wanduz 'fence' — Wiktionary: cognate with English wand, not wall. [wiktionary]

schmelzen.context_phrase: Der Schnee schmilzt in der Sonne.
schmelzen.context_translation: The snow melts in the sun.
schmelzen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *smeltaną — the page names English smelt as the cognate, a twin variant of melt; strong verb class 3: schmolz, geschmolzen. [wiktionary]

scham.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skamo — the page lists English shame as the direct cognate: the same word, sound for sound. [wiktionary]

laufen.context_phrase: Ich laufe jeden Morgen im Park.
laufen.context_translation: I run every morning in the park.
laufen.etymology_derivation: Class 7 strong verb from Proto-West Germanic *hlaupan - the exact relative of English leap and lope; läuft-lief-gelaufen preserves the old ablaut. [wiktionary]

bitten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *bidjaną — English bid is the documented cognate (Old English biddan); strong verb: bat, gebeten. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
